<!--
NUMBER PENDING, as for the other rebuilt supplements.

WHAT IT IS. One quantity over the whole plane: the standard error each member DELIVERS, the square
root of the diagonal of the distortion-corrected (sandwich) covariance, for all five parameters.

THE NESTING IS TRANSPOSED against Figure 4's: the PARAMETER owns the block and the members sit
side by side inside it (`outer = "param"`). Figure 4 nests member first because its question is
what one member reports; here the question is how the members COMPARE on the same error, and that
is answered by adjacency. With the members inside, the five columns of a block are five estimates
of the same number and the eye does the comparison; with the members outside, comparing k_off
across members means jumping over four other parameters each time. The column count is identical
either way, 22, so the transposition is free: LSE is absent from three of the five blocks and
present in two.

WHY THE CORRECTED ONE AND NOT WHAT THE MEMBER REPORTS. The reported covariance is what the
algorithm CLAIMS, and Figure 4's second moment spends its panels showing that claim to be wrong by
up to 74x. The corrected one is the sandwich estimate of the estimator's true variance, so it is
the only version in which a cross-member comparison is apples to apples: it says what each method
actually achieves, not what it asserts. Same rule as Figure 5.

A SEQUENTIAL SCALE, AND WHY THE SHARED ONE WAS WRONG HERE. Every other figure on this plane draws
a quantity whose null is 1 and which can err in EITHER direction, so it takes a diverging scale
with white at the null. A standard error cannot go below its null: 1 is a parameter known exactly
and there is no "conservative" side to colour blue. Half of a diverging scale would be dead, and
the eye would read the pale end as "calibrated" when here it means "measured". So this figure uses
`SCALE_SE`: pale for a parameter pinned, dark for one barely determined, monotone in luminance so
it survives greyscale and any colour vision.

THE TWO CRITERIA ARE UNCHANGED, which is the point of keeping them: 1.15 and 2 are band EDGES and
carry the same solid and dashed marks as everywhere else in the set. Here they read as "the error
bar is 15 per cent of the parameter" and "the error bar is a factor two", which is exactly what the
white contour pair meant on the body figure. Those white contours are turned off here
(`se_lines = FALSE`): they would trace the boundary of the very field they sit on.

THE BANDS REACH BELOW 1.02, and that is why this figure has a scale of its own, `SCALE_SE`, and
does not share `SCALE_ONESIDED` with the autocorrelation panel. The useful range of a standard
error goes down to a few per mil: the closing rate at ten thousand channels is 0.0016 to 0.0071 in
log10 units, a factor 1.004 to 1.016, so a first edge at 1.02 painted that entire column one flat
band and the figure lost exactly the comparison it exists to make.

WHERE the extra cuts go was itself measured, and the first attempt had them in the wrong place.
Cuts at 1.002 and 1.005 open nothing: only 11 of 5725 cells fall below 1.01 at all. What is
populated is the band they were meant to split, (1.01, 1.02], which holds 217 of the 247 k_off
cells at ten thousand channels, and the cut that splits THAT is 1.015 — 102 cells below it against
231 below 1.02. So the ladder is 1.005 as a floor marker, then 1.01 and 1.015 doing the work.
Nothing from 1.02 up moves, so this scale and `SCALE_ONESIDED` agree wherever they overlap and
1.15 and 2 are members of both.

One thing no scale will fix, and it is the result rather than a defect: at ten thousand channels
k_off runs 1.0032 (MR) to 1.0187 (NR) across the seven members, all inside 1.5 per cent of each
other. That column comes out nearly uniform because the members ARE nearly equal there.

ABOVE THE TOP EDGE THE CELLS ARE GREY, NOT DARK, and that is a statement rather than a rendering
choice. Measured over the source data, 608 of 5725 cells (10.6 per cent) exceed a factor 1000, they
sit in the unitary current and the channel number for every member, and the largest is a factor
10^19115: past a point the design simply does not determine the parameter and the sandwich is
unbounded. Painting those the darkest band would say "very large", which is a claim about a number
that has no scale; grey says "not measurable here", which is what is true.

The grey is a TERMINAL BAND OF THE SCALE, not a layer of marks stamped over the field, and that is
what makes it continuous: the same contour draws it, so its edge is exactly where the value
crosses a factor 1000 and it joins up the way every other band does. A first attempt stamped one
rectangle per off-scale cell and the result was a lattice of little blocks that read as data. As a
band it also appears in the COLOUR BAR, at the far end past 10^3, where it explains itself without
a second key.

THE X AXIS IS DRAWN ONCE, bottom left, for the same reason the nesting was transposed. A ggplot
scale belongs to every facet column of its block, so tick labels on a five-column block print five
times and, with the panels flush, the "1" of one column lands on the "0.01" of the next. That never
showed while the labelled block was LSE with its single column. All 22 columns carry the identical
range, so one labelled axis serves them and the blocks keep their ticks without numbers.

Below that the bands stay coarse from 2 up: the third quartile of the corrected standard error is
a factor 1.9 for LSE and 200 for NR, and a scale that chased the tail would flatten everything
below 2, which is where the comparison lives.

WHAT THE FIGURE DROPS, and where to find it. An earlier draft of this file had two sides, the
REPORTED standard error against the delivered one, and the contrast was the strongest single
result in the set. It is recorded here so that dropping the panel does not drop the finding.
Medians over the seven intervals at noise 0.1, in log10 units of the parameter:

                       N_ch:      10       100      1000     10000
    k_off  reported    LSE     0.0796   0.0236   0.0074   0.0023
                       NR      0.0481   0.0183   0.0063   0.0020
                       INR     0.0427   0.0151   0.0050   0.0016
                       R       0.1634   0.0527   0.0167   0.0052
                       IR      0.1707   0.0621   0.0198   0.0063
           delivered   LSE     0.2172   0.0658   0.0207   0.0066
                       NR      0.2106   0.0692   0.0219   0.0071
                       INR     0.2129   0.0686   0.0217   0.0069
                       R       0.1795   0.0615   0.0199   0.0063
                       IR      0.1787   0.0614   0.0199   0.0063

On the closing rate every member DELIVERS the same precision to within twelve per cent, and what
separates them is entirely what they CLAIM: least squares understates by a factor 2.9, the
open-loop pair by 3.5 and 4.3, the recursive filter by 1.2, and the boundary-conditioned one
claims what it delivers. So on a rate the likelihood family does not buy a better estimate, it
buys a truthful error bar. The ratio of the two blocks is the MARGINAL distortion,
sqrt(diag(F^-1 J F^-1) / diag(F^-1)), which is not Figure 4's map, diag(F^-1/2 J F^-1/2): the
marginal reading is systematically milder and the two must not be quoted as the same number.

The channel-number direction says the opposite and is drawn here: the recursion buys real
precision there, 0.075 and 0.070 against 0.291 and 0.223 at ten thousand channels, a factor four.
A rate lives in the shape of the transient, which everyone gets; the count lives in the
fluctuation amplitude, which an open-loop predictor throws away.

LSE CARRIES TWO COLUMNS AND NOT FIVE, and the reason is not coverage. nonlinearsqr indexes its own
four parameters and they do not line up with the macro ones: its index 2 is Current_Baseline and
its 3 is Num_ch_mean, where the macro members have unitary_current and Current_Noise. Left alone,
the shared index-to-name mapping would have drawn LSE's channel number inside the sigma_noise
panel. Excluded in EXCLUDE_ROWS with the note; the like-for-like argument agrees, since LSE holds
the unitary current fixed and has no free noise scale.
-->

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

```{r common, include=FALSE}
# ROSTER CORRECTED 2026-08-11 (Luciano), the same repair as figure_4_supplement_sample_corr.Rmd
# and for the same reason: this file was rendered 2026-08-02 and the un-averaged least-squares arm
# `nonlinearsqr_g` was added on 2026-08-05 (commit a202e03, the only directory carrying it), so
# the roster was five and `nonlinearsqr` was labelled LSE when that token is ILSE. Now identical
# to figure_4.Rmd:327-332. Both least-squares arms are excluded by EXCLUDE_ROWS from every block
# but the two rates, so this adds columns to the k_on and k_off blocks only.
FIG4_ALGOS     <- c("nonlinearsqr_g", "nonlinearsqr", "macro_NR", "macro_INR",
                    "macro_R", "macro_IR")
FIG4_ALGO_LAB  <- c(nonlinearsqr_g = "LSE", nonlinearsqr = "ILSE", macro_NR = "NR",
                    macro_INR = "INR", macro_R = "R", macro_IR = "IR")
FIG4_DATA_DIRS <- c("../data/1c2ae6f", "../data/87889e6", "../data/0ffbda7", "../data/1f7138b",
                    "../data/a202e03")
# all five, kinetic first, then the two amplitude directions, then the noise scale
# with outer = "param" these name the BLOCKS, and the members become the columns inside each
FIG4_PARS   <- c("on", "off", "unitary_current", "Current_Noise", "Num_ch_mean")
FIG4_PSHORT <- c(on = "k[on]", off = "k[off]", unitary_current = "i",
                 Current_Noise = "sigma[noise]", Num_ch_mean = "N[ch]")
source("figure_4_common.R")
source("figure_4_layout.R")
```

```{r sides}
# One side. The diagonal of the corrected covariance, square-rooted, IS the fill: the scale is
# log10 of a factor and a standard error in log10 units of the parameter already is one, so `zf`
# is the identity on it and no transform is hidden anywhere.
# From the shared source data: the standard error product is already the diagonal of the corrected
# covariance, square-rooted, one row per (member, cell, interval, parameter).
sedel <- dplyr::filter(.fig4_src$sedat, algo %in% ALGOS) %>% dplyr::rename(se = sev)

SIDES <- list(
  list(lab = "distortion-corrected standard error, in log10 units of the parameter",
       letter = "A", data = sedel, zf = function(x) x$se,
       # past the top edge the cell is greyed, not painted the end band: see the header
       scale = SCALE_SE, grey_offscale = TRUE))
```

```{r render, fig.width = 7.4, fig.height = 4.90}
# RECALIBRATED 2026-08-11 with the corrected roster. 24 columns now, not 22: the un-averaged
# least-squares arm adds one column to each of the two rate blocks and none elsewhere. The old
# knob 0.1609 was measured against 22 columns (x 0.1400, y 0.1400) and left this render 9.1 per
# cent tall once the columns narrowed to x 0.1283, so it is rescaled by that ratio,
# 0.1609 x 0.1283 / 0.1400 = 0.1475. Verify with `python3 tmp/measure_fig4.py <pdf>` against a
# target of 100 per cent, and do not trust the nominal: the layout heights are null units.
# THE COST, and it is the real objection to this page: five parameter blocks across 7.4 in put the
# cell under a millimetre, against 1.14 mm on the body figure. Narrowest in the set.
fig4_render(SIDES, per_row = 0.1475, out = "Figure_4_S4.pdf",
            se_lines = FALSE, key = FALSE, outer = "param", drawn_axis = TRUE)
```

```{r what-each-axis-buys}
# WHAT EACH DESIGN AXIS BUYS, measured, because the readings below were argued from the picture and
# from first principles and neither is evidence. Two questions, both asked of the same object the
# figure fills with, `sedel$se`, the distortion-corrected standard error in log10 units of the
# parameter. Nothing here is a new computation; it is the field the panels draw, summarised.
#
# Q1. IS THE NOISE PARAMETER'S ERROR SET BY THE INTERVAL AND NOT BY THE NOISE? The prediction is
# that it is, and it is the cheapest thing in the figure to teach the axes with: sigma is the scale
# of a WHITE process, so its relative error goes as 1/sqrt(2N) with N the sample count, T/Delta.
# That has two consequences and both are testable here. Flat in the noise level, since a scale
# parameter's relative error does not depend on its own value. And going as sqrt(Delta), so the
# log-log slope against the interval is +0.5.
# EXCLUDE_ROWS IS NOT OPTIONAL HERE, and the first run of this chunk proved it. The least-squares
# arms index their OWN four parameters and the mapping does not line up: `nonlinearsqr`'s index 3
# is Num_ch_mean where the macro members have Current_Noise, so the shared index-to-name map files
# LSE's CHANNEL NUMBER under sigma_noise. Reading it as the noise gave a slope of -0.007 against
# the interval, which looked like a finding and was a mislabelled parameter. The panels never show
# it because EXCLUDE_ROWS drops both arms from this block; this chunk has to drop them too.
se_noise <- dplyr::filter(sedel, param == "Current_Noise", is.finite(se), se > 0) %>%
  dplyr::anti_join(EXCLUDE_ROWS, by = c("algo", "param"))
cat("\n=== Q1a. sigma_noise: spread of the standard error ACROSS noise levels,\n",
    "         at fixed member, N_ch and interval (0 = perfectly flat) ===\n", sep = "")
se_noise %>%
  dplyr::group_by(algo, Num_ch, interval_in_tau) %>%
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::n() >= 3) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(n_noise = dplyr::n(), rel_spread = sd(se) / mean(se), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::group_by(algo) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(cells = dplyr::n(), median_rel_spread = median(rel_spread),
                   max_rel_spread = max(rel_spread), .groups = "drop") %>%
  as.data.frame() %>% print(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

cat("\n=== Q1b. sigma_noise: log-log slope of the standard error against the interval\n",
    "         (prediction +0.5 if it is 1/sqrt(sample count)) ===\n", sep = "")
se_noise %>%
  dplyr::group_by(algo, Num_ch, noise) %>%
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::n() >= 3) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(slope = coef(lm(log10(se) ~ log10(interval_in_tau)))[2], .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::group_by(algo) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(fits = dplyr::n(), median_slope = median(slope),
                   q10 = quantile(slope, 0.1), q90 = quantile(slope, 0.9), .groups = "drop") %>%
  as.data.frame() %>% print(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

# Q2. WHAT DOES SAMPLING FASTER BUY, and where? The ratio of the standard error at the coarsest
# swept interval to the one at the finest, per parameter and per noise level, at the largest patch.
# 1 means the extra samples bought nothing; 10 would be the full 1/sqrt(N) of a hundredfold change
# in Delta. Anything between is the autocorrelation eating the extra samples: averaging n samples of
# a correlated process divides the variance by n/tau_int and not by n.
D_LO <- min(sedel$interval_in_tau); D_HI <- max(sedel$interval_in_tau)
cat("\n=== Q2. gain from sampling at Delta = ", D_LO, " instead of ", D_HI,
    ", as se(coarse)/se(fine), at N_ch = 10^4 ===\n", sep = "")
sedel %>%
  dplyr::anti_join(EXCLUDE_ROWS, by = c("algo", "param")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(Num_ch == 10000, interval_in_tau %in% c(D_LO, D_HI), is.finite(se), se > 0) %>%
  dplyr::select(algo, param, noise, interval_in_tau, se) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = interval_in_tau, values_from = se,
                     names_prefix = "D_") %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data[[paste0("D_", D_LO)]]), !is.na(.data[[paste0("D_", D_HI)]])) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(gain = .data[[paste0("D_", D_HI)]] / .data[[paste0("D_", D_LO)]]) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(param, noise) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(members = dplyr::n(), median_gain = median(gain), .groups = "drop") %>%
  # ONLY THE COLUMNS EVERY MEMBER REACHES. The three non-decade noise levels (0.05, 0.2, 0.5) are
  # run for ONE member and not six, so their median is that member's value and is not comparable
  # with the rest. The first run of this chunk printed them beside the others and the 0.2 column
  # came out at twice its neighbours in EVERY parameter at once, which is what a coverage artefact
  # looks like and what a physical effect does not.
  dplyr::group_by(noise) %>% dplyr::filter(max(members) >= 4) %>% dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = noise, values_from = median_gain, id_cols = param,
                     names_prefix = "z_") %>%
  as.data.frame() %>% print(digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

cat("\n(the three non-decade noise levels are one member only and are dropped from the table above;\n",
    " the lowest level every member reaches is the label 0.1, i.e. S_tilde = 0.01)\n", sep = "")
```
